name: Ingenuity Mars Helicopter

location.name: "Valinor Hills", Ingenuity's final airfield (Flight 72), Jezero crater

headline: The first aircraft to fly on another world, grounded on a Martian sand ripple
story: Ingenuity reached Mars on 18 February 2021, folded beneath the belly of the Perseverance rover in Jezero crater. On 19 April 2021, the 1.8-kilogram helicopter rose 3 meters into the thin air, hovered, and settled back down: the first powered, controlled flight on another planet. It carried a small swatch of muslin from the wing of the Wright brothers' Flyer 1.

It was built for up to five test flights over 30 days. Instead it flew for almost three years: 72 flights, more than two hours aloft, about 17 kilometers covered. On 18 January 2024, over a stretch of smooth, featureless sand, its navigation system lost track of the ground. Ingenuity came down hard on the slope of a ripple, and its rotor blades broke.

NASA ended the mission on 25 January 2024. The team nicknamed the spot Valinor Hills, after a place in J.R.R. Tolkien's novels. Ingenuity still stands there, tilted near the crest of a sand ripple, with a piece of one blade lying about 15 meters to the west. It has become a stationary testbed, waking to record temperatures and photograph the sand around it.

facts.label: First flight

facts.value: Up to 5 test flights over 30 days

facts.label: Flown

images.caption: 19 April 2021: seen by Perseverance's Navcam from 64 meters away, Ingenuity hovers above Jezero crater on the first powered, controlled flight on another planet.
4 February 2024: from about 450 meters away, Perseverance's Mastcam-Z finds Ingenuity at its final airfield, Valinor Hills, after the hard landing of Flight 72. Enhanced color.
24 February 2024: Perseverance's SuperCam zooms in from 415 meters. Ingenuity stands tilted near the crest of a ripple (right); a large piece of a rotor blade lies about 15 meters to the west.
